diagram.documentation:
The top levels of the stereotype definition breakdown structure for the MBOE mapping relations extensions.

Combined mapping relations are not shown. For the full set of mapping relations see mappingRelation - Full relationship stereotypes inheritance

A complete set of overlapping diagrams showing parts of the breakdown structure is provided to help with readability. These are all in the same package as this diagram and have names prefixed with mappingRelation. For an overview of all mappingRelation diagrams, see Section 7 in the Model Guide - Read Me First

 

When CCM transforms OWL ontologies as they are imported from RDF to UML, any RDF properties that the transformer doesn't recognize are rendered as UML associations. This works well for most relations (because a lot of relations in UML models tend to be associations), but it is problematic when the semantics of the property would be better represented with a standard UML relationship other than association. In this model, this applies in particular to relationships that indicate that one element depends on another (e.g. a definition adopted from another vocabulary), which are more naturally represented as UML dependencies. UML associations do not have an attribute that can be used to indicate either general directionality or dependency: the only support for directional attributes is for reading direction (which does not suffice as an assertion of dependency) and navigability (which is a dependency, but only applies to efficiency of runtime access).

 

There is no way for the importer to know the semantics of the imported property automatically (without connecting it to some kind of reasoning engine). This means that the semantics must be applied manually by human review of the model. There are several possible ways to resolve this.

  • Repurpose the navigability property to indicate a directional association
    • This is a fairly common informal practice adopted by many modelers in search of a way to add an arrowhead to an association, but has several drawbacks. The UML 2.5.1 specification states that "Navigability means that instances participating in links at runtime (instances of an Association) can be accessed efficiently from instances at the other ends of the Association". For conceptual modeling, this is not a particular useful property, so within controlled contexts (e.g. a model used only by a single organization) it can be acceptable to redefine the meaning of the navigability arrowhead, provided everyone working on the model is made aware. Because the intended output of this model is a broadly useful UML profile for modeling multiple contexts, this is not an appropriate choice here.
  • Manually refactor the type on the each imported relationship (e.g. change its type from association to dependency)
    • This could cause compatibility problems if the model is used to generate 'round trip' outputs to RDF because information is potentially lost (associations have a different set of attributes than dependencies).
  • Establish newly created "mirror" relationships with the correct type (e.g. dependency) in the metamodel, with traceability links to the property that was imported as an association.
    • This approach is time consuming, increases the maintenance burden, and generates unnecessary duplication.
  • Retain Association as the base type and extend this through inheritance of additional properties through multiple inheritance (e.g. those relationships that are dependencies would have stereotypes «association» and «dependency»).
    • This is a fairly clean solution, but it is not parsimonious because the relationships inherit additional properties that are not strictly necessary. This potentially undermines the benefits of the separation of concerns implicit in the intentional disjointedness of these metaclasses in the UML specification.
  • The cleanest, most parsimonious solution identified, which is used here, is to define custom stereotypes based on standard UML metaclasses in a profile based on the metamodel (see mappingRelation - Top levels).
    • Custom stereotypes ensure that the relationships only have the required properties from the relevant metaclasses. This avoids unnecessary multiple inheritance.

Adopting this final approach means that it is not possible to define relationships based on the custom stereotypes in the metamodel, because this would otherwise create a circular dependency by applying a stereotype in the model that is also defined by the same model. Avoiding this ensures a degree of self-bootstrapping, in that the model can be loaded without needing to preload any profiles to support custom types (except those used from the CCM profile) and can generate the MBOE profile from only standard UML metaclasses.

 

One side effect of the adopted approach is that it is not possible to represent the extensions to skos:mappingRelation directly in the UML metamodel, because CCM converts all the relevant RDF object properties to associations. The disadvantage is that the metamodel does not contain elements representing all the relationships defined in the MBOE profile. Instead, these are declared only as stereotypes on profile diagrams. To assert the mappings from the profile to the metamodel, UML realization relationships (a type of dependency) are shown from top level stereotype elements (which have various metaclasses declared here) to the corresponding imported RDF properties (which are all of type association) in diagram mappingRelation - SKOS to profile mapping. Note also that the type inheritance structure shown here deviates from the the SKOS/core RDF specification relating to the range of the imported element Association[Concept -> is in mapping relation with:Thing], which it is understood should have a narrower range of 'Concept -> is in mapping relation with: Concept' - for details see: SKOS Metamodel - Per RDF classes and associations (no annotations).
